title: THz-induced phonon mode mixing and collective dynamics in a polar nanolattice
authors: Elizabeth Skoropata, Peter M. Derlet, Hiroki Ueda, Roman Mankowsky, Mathias Sander, Henrik T. Lemke, Rafael T. Winkler, Yunpei Deng, Milan Radovic, Matteo Savoini, Biaolong Liu, Martina Basini, Vladimir Ovuka, Steven L. Johnson, Marta D. Rossell, Urs Staub
abstract: Manipulating phonons through symmetry is a fundamental approach to alter the dynamic responses of materials. Most often new phases are sought through control of the unit-cell (e.g. via strain, doping, light, etc.). By comparison, there is vast potential to look beyond the unit-cell into higher-order architectures to control wave scattering and interference effects that remains less explored. We describe the THz-induced dynamics of an SrTiO$_{3}$ thin film with a nanoscale ordered interfacial dislocation network probed with 2- and 3-dimensional time-resolved x-ray diffraction and classical molecular dynamics simulations. We find that symmetry breaking at all scales is an effective approach to create a dynamical electric polarization and to control phonon mixing that generates previously unreported collective modes in the THz regime with circular vortex-like displacements. This work opens a new pathway to explore dynamical functional properties that can be extended to magnetic, electric, and ferroelectric systems by controlling the real-space topology via epitaxy.
summary: This paper explores using nanoscale structural imperfections, specifically dislocation networks in STO thin films, to control phonon behavior. By exciting the material with THz pulses and measuring the resulting X-ray diffraction changes, the authors show that symmetry breaking generates novel collective vibrational modes. This opens a new avenue for designing functional materials by controlling their real-space topology.
main_problem: The study investigates how controlling symmetry breaking at nanoscale interfaces, such as dislocation networks, can be used to manipulate phonon mode mixing and generate novel collective dynamics in polar materials.
main_result: Symmetry breaking due to dislocations induces a mixture of acoustic and optical modes, leading to measurable dynamic electric polarization and the generation of previously unobserved collective THz-frequency modes.
method: The research combines ultrafast time-resolved X-ray diffraction (tr-XRD) experiments using THz pulses with classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Strontium Titanate ($	ext{SrTiO}_3$) thin film grown on a complex substrate, engineered to contain an ordered network of interfacial misfit dislocations. Simulations model the lattice response under strain and electric fields.
key_observables: Transient diffraction intensity ($\Delta I/I$), out-of-plane vs. in-plane atomic displacements, dynamic electric polarization ($|P|$), and vorticity measures ($\lambda_2$).
important_parameters: THz frequency regime (e.g., 0.060 to 0.124 THz modes); nanoscale structural features like dislocation spacing; picosecond time scales.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on drawing analogies from fluid dynamics concepts (helicity, $\lambda_2$) and comparing simulation results with experimental measurements despite differences in system size or boundary conditions.
figures_summary: Figures show STEM images of dislocation networks, time-resolved XRD intensity changes at Bragg/satellite reflections, simulated atomic displacement patterns comparing pristine vs. dislocated films, and FFT spectra confirming mode mixing.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the experimental setup (tr-XRD on STO/dislocations), presenting key findings regarding symmetry breaking effects observed in diffraction data, supporting these results with detailed MD simulations, and concluding with a generalized pathway for controlling dynamical functional properties via real-space topology.
why_interesting: The work demonstrates how engineered structural defects can act as powerful tuning knobs for lattice dynamics, offering an analogy to controlling quantum states or excitations by manipulating the underlying geometry of a solid-state system.
